headline: Alder Compliance's every checkable number lands inside the independently estimated range, and the deck names its own biggest risk unprompted — the open question is whether 'depth' survives two heavily funded leaders who are already doing the down-market move the deck describes as hypothetical.

verdict.confidence_rationale: Market size, growth, serviceable slice, competitive framing, open-source boundary, retention and CAC payback are each supported by the research [S1][S2][S3]. That is unusual and it is evidence about the founders as well as about the market. Confidence is medium rather than high because the two things that would decide the investment are the two the deck omits: who the team is, and what 'depth' concretely means. The research also leaves the decisive competitive question open — it does not say how far the leaders' down-market move has already gone.

scorecard.rationale: The deck claims $2.8B in 2025 growing roughly 22%; independent estimates give $2.6-3.0B with 20-24% growth [S1]. The serviceable slice claimed — 'closer to $340M' for Series A to Series C startups in North America — sits inside the $300-400M the research gives for that same segment definition [S1]. Every figure is inside its range. Scored 6 rather than higher because an accurate $340M is still a small market: the sizing is honest and the ceiling is real.
evidence: $2.6-3.0B for 2025, 20-24% growth, Series A-C North America segment plausibly $300-400M [S1]

scorecard.rationale: The deck's description is accurate — Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders, both heavily funded [S2] — and it concedes their dominance rather than dismissing it. The correction runs the other way from usual: the deck presents Vanta moving down-market as a future possibility, and the research reports both leaders already extending toward earlier-stage companies [S2]. The market analysis rates absorption as 'contested' on a 2-3 year horizon, driven by competitive compression rather than platform bundling, which is slower but aimed directly at the segment Alder occupies.
evidence: Both leaders extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2]

scorecard.rationale: 'Depth for a narrower customer profile' carries the entire differentiation and is never defined. The deck concedes on slide 6 that depth is defensible but not permanent, which is the right reading, and the market analysis agrees for a specific reason: depth is the class of advantage a funded competitor with more engineers closes fastest [S2]. No product mechanism is described anywhere.
evidence: No product description in the deck

scorecard.rationale: Competes on price and never states a price. CAC payback of 14 months sits inside the 12-18 month normal band [S3]. $520k across 41 customers implies roughly $12.7k each — arithmetic on the deck's behalf, not a stated figure. No gross margin. The research could establish no absolute price levels for the category, so there is no benchmark against which to test the price claim even if one were given.
evidence: 12-18 months is within the normal band [S3]

scorecard.rationale: $520k ARR, 41 customers, 8% MoM sustained six months, 104% NRR, 14-month payback. Six months is long enough to be a trend, and volunteering retention is unusual. The market analysis supplies the necessary qualification: NRR above 100% is typical for compliance vendors serving growing startups, because customers add frameworks as they grow [S3]. So 104% confirms the business is behaving normally rather than outperforming, and sits at the low end of normal.
evidence: NRR above 100% typical; CAC payback 12-18 months normal [S3]

scorecard.rationale: No founders, no backgrounds, no headcount, no advisors. In a deck this forthcoming the omission is conspicuous, and at seed the team is most of what is being underwritten.
evidence: No team information in the deck

scorecard.rationale: $4M at $20M post is $16M pre on $520k ARR, roughly 31x — high, but lower than most decks at this stage attempt, and the research offers no valuation benchmark either way [S1]. Unlike most, the milestone is stated and checkable: $2M ARR in 24 months, which from $520k at the stated 8% MoM is reachable well inside the window. Use of funds is still missing.
evidence: Deck slide 5: 8% MoM for six months
No valuation norms available for this category

claim_audit.claim: The compliance automation market was $2.8B in 2025 growing at roughly 22% a year according to independent analyst estimates
claim_audit.market_evidence: Independent estimates put compliance automation at $2.6-3.0B for 2025 with growth of 20-24% annually [S1].
claim_audit.delta: $2.8B is the midpoint of the range; 22% is inside the band. No material gap.
claim_audit.so_what: The market slide can be taken at face value, which is itself a signal about how this team sources figures.

claim_audit.claim: Our serviceable slice — startups between Series A and Series C in North America — is closer to $340M
claim_audit.market_evidence: The Series A to Series C North America startup segment is plausibly $300-400M [S1].
claim_audit.delta: $340M sits inside $300-400M, and the deck's segment definition matches the one the research sizes.
claim_audit.so_what: Honestly stated and small. $340M is the ceiling on the segment, and the deck never confronts what that implies for a venture outcome.

claim_audit.claim: Vanta and Drata dominate this category and are both well funded
claim_audit.market_evidence: Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders in compliance automation, both heavily funded [S2].
claim_audit.delta: None. The deck names its two strongest competitors and concedes their position.
claim_audit.so_what: A competition slide that concedes is a different underwriting object from one that deflects.

claim_audit.claim: Open-source tooling exists but does not produce auditor-ready evidence
claim_audit.market_evidence: Open-source alternatives exist for control monitoring but do not produce auditor-ready evidence packages [S2].
claim_audit.delta: None; the deck's characterisation matches the research almost word for word.
claim_audit.so_what: It also locates where the paid value sits. The market analysis reads this as mild rather than severe pricing pressure precisely because open source stopped at the monitoring layer, and it identifies the evidence package as the durable asset — durable against open source, less so against two funded leaders who already produce it.

claim_audit.market_evidence: NRR above 100% is typical for compliance vendors serving growing startups, as customers add frameworks over time [S3].
claim_audit.delta: Above 100% and therefore normal — at the low end of what 'typical' implies rather than a standout.
claim_audit.so_what: Confirms health without demonstrating an edge. Ask how much of the 4% is framework attach versus seat growth.

claim_audit.market_evidence: CAC payback of 12-18 months is within the normal band [S3].
claim_audit.so_what: Efficient enough that the round can fund growth rather than repair acquisition.

claim_audit.claim: Vanta could move down-market at any time; our differentiation is depth, which is defensible but not permanent
claim_audit.market_evidence: Both Vanta and Drata have been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2].
claim_audit.delta: The risk the deck frames as conditional is reported as already in progress, and it applies to both leaders rather than one.
claim_audit.so_what: Right about the mechanism, behind on the timing. This moves from a risk to monitor to a condition to test now — and the research does not say how far the move has gone, which is the gap that matters most.

claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses this company's revenue.
claim_audit.delta: Not checkable externally; well specified for the stage.
claim_audit.so_what: Straightforward diligence given the level of detail already offered.

claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses this company's growth.
claim_audit.delta: Six months is a long enough window to be a trend rather than a spike.
claim_audit.so_what: Confirm month-by-month; it is the basis of the stated 24-month milestone.

claim_audit.claim: Collecting SOC2 evidence takes an engineer roughly six weeks of part-time work spread over a quarter
claim_audit.delta: Plausible and specific; the research does not reach it.
claim_audit.so_what: Ask whether it comes from customer data or founder experience.

claim_audit.claim: Raising $4M at $20M post to reach $2M ARR in 24 months
claim_audit.market_evidence: No valuation or funding data for this category was available [S1][S2].
claim_audit.delta: About 31x ARR, with a milestone that is arithmetically reachable at the stated growth rate.
claim_audit.so_what: The plan is checkable, which is more than most decks offer. Whether 31x is the right price cannot be settled from the available evidence.

where_deck_matches_market: Serviceable slice: $340M claimed, $300-400M estimated on the same segment definition [S1].
Competitive framing: Vanta and Drata named as dominant and heavily funded [S2].
Open source: exists for control monitoring, does not produce auditor-ready evidence — stated by both in near-identical terms [S2].
Retention and payback: 104% NRR and 14-month payback both inside category norms [S3].
where_deck_overstates: Nothing material. On every claim the research reaches, the deck is inside the independently estimated range.
where_deck_understates: Competitive timing: the deck says Vanta 'could' move down-market; both leaders already are [S2]. Understating a threat is rarer than overstating an opportunity and is the one place the deck is behind its own evidence.

The open-source boundary as an asset. The deck states it as a fact about competitors; the market analysis reads it as the location of the durable value — the evidence package is defensible against open source because auditor acceptance is not something a project can ship [S2]. That is an argument the deck could be making about itself.

blind_spots.what: Both Vanta and Drata — not only Vanta — are already extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck treats this as a future risk from one competitor. It is a present condition from both, and it compresses the window in which price-and-depth remains an available position.

blind_spots.what: 104% NRR is typical rather than distinguishing, because compliance customers add frameworks as they grow.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck offers retention as evidence of product strength. The category gets that lift structurally, so the figure shows normal behaviour at the low end of normal rather than an edge.

blind_spots.what: $340M is the ceiling on the whole segment.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck is right about the number and never confronts it. $2M ARR needs 0.6% of the segment and is plausible; a fund-returning outcome needs a share a fourth entrant rarely gets, or an expansion path beyond the segment. Neither is addressed.

blind_spots.what: The research does not say how far the leaders' down-market move has already gone, and names no open-source project or adoption figure.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: Those are the two facts that would settle the investment question, and neither is available. This report's own confidence is bounded by that, not only the deck's.

risks.risk: Vanta and Drata complete the down-market move and remove the price-and-depth position
risks.mitigation_or_test: Win rate and price against each over the last two quarters [S2].

risks.risk: 'Depth' is a feature set rather than a moat and is matched within a release cycle
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask the founders to name three things they do that Vanta cannot, and check each against Vanta's current product.

risks.risk: The $340M segment ceiling caps the outcome below what the round requires
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask for the expansion path beyond Series A-C North America [S1].

risks.risk: 104% NRR erodes as cohorts age past the framework-addition phase
risks.mitigation_or_test: NRR by cohort age rather than in aggregate [S3].

risks.risk: Open-source control monitoring advances into the evidence layer
risks.mitigation_or_test: The research names no project and gives no trend [S2] — worth establishing directly, since the whole pricing-pressure read rests on that boundary holding.

risks.risk: The team is unknown and may not execute against two funded leaders

questions: Both leaders are already extending down-market — what has that done to your win rate and price in the last two quarters? [S2]
Name the three things your depth does that Vanta cannot do today.
How much of your 104% NRR is framework attach versus seat expansion? [S3]
$340M is the whole segment; what is the path beyond it? [S1]
Who is the team, and have they sold to this buyer before?
What is your actual price, given price is half your differentiation?
Which open-source projects do you see in deals, and how often? [S2]
What happens to the 24-month plan if growth falls to 5% MoM?

actions.action: Request founder backgrounds — the one missing input on an otherwise checkable deck
Test the depth claim feature-by-feature against Vanta's current product
Get win/loss history with prices covering the period of the leaders' down-market move [S2]
Reference three customers on why they chose Alder over the leaders
Model the outcome against the $340M ceiling and ask for the expansion thesis [S1]
Establish which open-source projects appear in deals — the research could not name any, and the pricing-pressure read depends on that boundary [S2]

summary:
Alder Compliance sells SOC2 evidence collection to startups approaching Series A. $520k ARR across 41 customers, 8% month-over-month growth sustained over six months, 104% net revenue retention, 14-month CAC payback, raising $4M at $20M post to reach $2M ARR in 24 months.

The unusual property of this deck is that its numbers survive checking. Compliance automation was $2.6-3.0B in 2025 growing 20-24%; the deck says $2.8B and roughly 22% [S1]. The Series A to Series C North America segment is plausibly $300-400M; the deck says 'closer to $340M' [S1]. Retention above 100% is typical for the category and CAC payback of 12-18 months is normal; the deck reports 104% and 14 months [S3]. Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders, both heavily funded, and the deck says so [S2]. Open-source alternatives exist for control monitoring but do not produce auditor-ready evidence packages, and the deck says that too, almost word for word [S2]. Slide 6 then volunteers the single most dangerous risk to the business — that Vanta could move down-market, and that depth is defensible but not permanent. Very few decks name their own kill shot.

The research corrects the deck once, and in the direction that matters. Both leaders — not one — have already been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2]. What the deck frames as a hypothetical is a present condition, and it is aimed at exactly the segment Alder holds. The market analysis reads this as competitive compression on a two-to-three-year horizon rather than platform absorption, which is slower and less total than being bundled into a suite, but it is pointed directly here.

Two qualifications temper the positive read, and both come from the research rather than the deck. First, 104% NRR is typical rather than distinguishing: compliance vendors serving growing startups get retention lift structurally as customers add frameworks [S3]. The figure confirms the business is behaving normally, at the low end of normal, and does not demonstrate an edge. Second, the deck is right about $340M without confronting what $340M means. Reaching $2M ARR takes 0.6% of the segment and is plausible; a fund-returning outcome needs either a share a fourth entrant rarely wins, or expansion beyond the segment, and neither appears.

There is also a structural insight in the evidence the deck states but does not use. Open source has reached the control-monitoring layer and stopped short of the auditor-ready evidence package [S2]. That places the paid value precisely: the evidence package is durable against open source, because its worth comes from auditor acceptance rather than from code, and auditor acceptance is not something a project can ship. It is considerably less durable against two funded leaders who already produce the same thing — which is why 'depth' needs a definition it never receives.

Against all of that, the deck contains no team slide at all. In a document this forthcoming that omission stands out, and at seed the team is most of what is being underwritten.

The call is YES WITH CONDITIONS. The single biggest reason to proceed is that everything checkable checks out, which is a fact about the market and a signal about the founders. The conditions are specific: founder backgrounds, and a feature-level defence of 'depth' against Vanta's current product, together with win/loss data covering the period in which both leaders moved down-market [S2]. What would flip it to a pass is finding that depth is a feature list rather than a structural advantage, or that win rates against the leaders have already begun to fall.
